1. The animation shows a street of houses with one dark house in the center, labeled "The darkest house" and dated June 2006. It seems to illustrate that someone who bought at the June 2006 peak ended up worse off than other buyers or renters. The houses on the right are brighter and the ones on the left are mid-gray. The header says the data comes from FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac rates. It is marked "ILLUSTRATIVE", "US only" and "history, not a forecast".

2. Only the text changes across the six frames. The label above the house goes from "The darkest house" in frames 1–2 to "$82,385 behind" in frames 3–6. The row of houses shifts slightly, with the white houses on the right and the lighter house on the left appearing to tilt or move a little. The June 2006 date and the dark house stay the same.

3. It means that a buyer in June 2006 is the "darkest" case in the historical data. Measured against renting and investing the money instead, they ended up $82,385 behind. Brighter houses presumably stand for better buy dates. The timing of a purchase can matter a lot, and buying is not always cheaper than renting.

4. A viewer might take away that buying does not always beat renting, and that purchase timing, prices, rents and mortgage rates all affect the result. The animation shows no recommendation, though. It doesn't say whether to rent or buy, and it explicitly says it is not a forecast.

5. The animation only suggests the idea that a 2006 purchase was the worst historical case, with an $82,385 shortfall. The caution that this is history and not a forecast is on screen. Any advice about renting versus buying today would be my own conclusion, and the on-screen text doesn't give it.
